title: Full-bleed chapters
why: Every section is a full-width band in its own colour, edge to edge, with the figures and the form both living on it. The page becomes five coloured chapters stacked in the order the money moves.
tradeoff: The boldest and the most memorable — you could tell where you are on this page from across the room. It also commits every input to a tinted surface, which is the thing to check: twelve expense fields on brick is a lot of red.

title: Coloured answer, paper working
why: Each section opens with a coloured band carrying only the headline figure and its three tiles. Everything you type or read in detail sits on paper directly below it, tied to the band by a matching edge.
tradeoff: The one I would build. It keeps the colour where it does the work — the answer — and keeps contrast where it is needed most, on the fields. It also gives every section the same two-part rhythm, so the page teaches you how to read it by the second scroll.

title: Inset slabs, like the hero
why: Not bands but rounded coloured cards, inset from the edge exactly as the hero is now — so the whole page reads as a series of objects on paper rather than stripes across it.
tradeoff: Closest to what is already live, and the least disruptive to build: the hero card already looks like this, so every other section just joins it. Loses the full-bleed drama that made option 1 land.

title: Paper page, coloured spine
why: The page stays on paper. Colour is spent on a thick left spine, the section rule, the headline figure and the tiles — enough to make each section unmistakably its own, without tinting a single field.
tradeoff: The quietest, and the strongest for long reading and data entry. Every figure sits on white at full contrast. The cost is that it never gives you the moment option 1 gave, where the surface itself changes under you.
